title: Conservation of biodiversity
summary: The forms biodiversity takes, the evidence that human activity is driving a biodiversity crisis, and the range of approaches used to conserve species and ecosystems.

keyterms.definition: The variety of life in all its forms, including ecosystem diversity, species diversity and genetic diversity.
The variety of different ecosystems or habitats in an area.
The variety of species in an area, taking into account both the number of species and their relative abundance.
The variety of alleles and genes within a species or population.
A geologically short period in which a large proportion of species become extinct; five have occurred in Earth's history.
Extinction caused by human activities, such as overhunting or habitat destruction, e.g. the moa and the Caribbean monk seal.
Destruction or conversion of a whole ecosystem, e.g. clearing of mixed dipterocarp forest in Southeast Asia for plantations.
Harvesting of a species by hunting, fishing or collecting faster than it can reproduce to replace losses.
A species introduced by humans to an area outside its natural range that spreads and harms native species or ecosystems.
Conservation of species in their natural habitat, e.g. by establishing and managing nature reserves.
Conservation of species outside their natural habitat, e.g. in zoos, botanic gardens or seed banks.
Restoring natural ecosystem processes, e.g. by reintroducing species such as apex predators and reducing human management.
Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered: species with few close relatives that are at high risk of extinction, prioritised for conservation.
Collection of scientific data by members of the public, e.g. species surveys that provide evidence of changes in biodiversity.

questions.prompt: Match each form of biodiversity to its description.

pairs.right: Variety of habitats in an area
Variety of species and their abundance
Variety of alleles within a species

questions.explanation: Biodiversity exists at three levels; conservation must protect all of them.

questions.statement: Genetic diversity within a species is part of biodiversity.
questions.explanation: Biodiversity includes genetic diversity. Populations with high genetic diversity are better able to adapt to changes such as new diseases.

questions.prompt: How many mass extinctions are recognised in Earth's history before the present?
options: One
Three
Five
Ten
questions.explanation: Five mass extinctions are recognised in the fossil record. Many scientists consider human activity to be causing a sixth.

questions.text: Extinction caused by human activities is described as ___ extinction.
questions.explanation: Anthropogenic means caused by humans. Current extinction rates are far above the natural background rate.

questions.prompt: Which is valid evidence for a biodiversity crisis?
options: One person reports seeing fewer birds in a garden
Repeated, large-scale surveys by scientists and citizen scientists showing declines in population sizes and ranges of many species
Some species have been newly described
Fossils show that extinctions occurred in the past
questions.explanation: Reliable evidence comes from systematic, repeated surveys over large areas, including citizen science, and assessments by expert bodies, showing widespread declines.

questions.statement: Citizen science cannot contribute useful data on biodiversity because it is collected by non-specialists.
questions.explanation: Large numbers of volunteers can survey wide areas over many years. With clear protocols and verification, citizen science provides valuable evidence of change.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the current number of species compared with the past is correct?
options: The number of species on Earth has never been higher than now and is still increasing rapidly
The number of species has been constant throughout Earth's history
Biodiversity was low before humans and humans have increased it
Overall biodiversity has increased over geological time, but human activity is now causing extinction rates far above background rates
questions.explanation: Despite setbacks from mass extinctions, life diversified over time. Today extinctions are occurring much faster than the background rate, leading to concern about a sixth mass extinction.

questions.text: The variety of life including ecosystems, species and genes is called ___.
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is short for biological diversity and covers all three levels.

questions.prompt: Why is species diversity not simply the number of species in an area?
options: It also considers the relative abundance of each species
It only counts endangered species
It counts the number of individuals of the commonest species
It ignores rare species
questions.explanation: Two areas with the same number of species can differ in diversity if one is dominated by a single species, so evenness (relative abundance) matters too.

questions.prompt: Order the levels of biodiversity from the broadest to the narrowest.
questions.explanation: Ecosystems contain many species, and each species contains genetic variation among its individuals.

lessons.title: Causes of extinction and ecosystem loss

questions.prompt: What was the main cause of the extinction of the moa in New Zealand?
options: Climate change at the end of the last ice age
An introduced disease from Europe
Competition with introduced mammals
Overhunting by humans after they settled New Zealand
questions.explanation: Moa were large flightless birds that had evolved without mammalian predators. They were hunted to extinction within a few centuries of human settlement.

questions.statement: The Caribbean monk seal became extinct mainly because of hunting by humans.
questions.explanation: It was hunted for its oil and skin and affected by overfishing of its prey; it has not been seen since the 1950s and was declared extinct in 2008.

questions.prompt: Which is the main cause of loss of mixed dipterocarp forest in Southeast Asia?
options: Logging and conversion of land to plantations such as oil palm
Volcanic eruptions
Invasion by grazing deer
Natural fires caused by lightning
questions.explanation: These tropical forests (e.g. in Borneo) have been cleared for timber and to grow crops such as oil palm, destroying the whole ecosystem.

questions.text: Hunting or fishing a species faster than it can reproduce is called ___.
questions.explanation: Overexploitation reduces populations below the level that can be sustained, and can lead to extinction.

questions.prompt: Match each cause of the biodiversity crisis to an example.

pairs.right: Forest cleared for oil palm plantations
Introduced rats eating eggs of island birds

questions.explanation: These causes, along with climate change, urbanization and human population growth, drive the current biodiversity crisis.

questions.statement: An invasive alien species is any species that is native to an area but has increased in number.
questions.explanation: Invasive alien species are introduced by humans from outside their natural range and spread to harm native species, e.g. by predation or competition.

questions.prompt: Why were island species such as the moa especially vulnerable to extinction after humans arrived?
options: They reproduced very quickly
They had evolved without mammalian predators, so had few defences and often reproduced slowly
They lived in very large populations across many continents
They were able to fly away from danger
questions.explanation: Isolated island species are often flightless, unafraid of predators and slow-breeding, with small ranges, so hunting or introduced predators quickly wipe them out.

questions.text: Species introduced outside their natural range that harm native species are called ___ alien species.
questions.explanation: Globalisation of trade and travel has spread many invasive species and diseases worldwide.

questions.prompt: Which underlying factor increases most other causes of biodiversity loss?
options: Growth of the human population and its demand for resources
Increasing numbers of nature reserves
Seed banking
Natural selection
questions.explanation: A larger human population needs more land, food, water and energy, driving habitat loss, overexploitation, pollution and climate change.

questions.prompt: Order the chain of events in loss of a rainforest ecosystem.
items: Demand for timber and palm oil increases
Habitat for forest species is lost
Forest-dependent species decline or become extinct
questions.explanation: Ecosystem loss removes the habitat many species depend on, so whole communities are lost together.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of in situ conservation?
options: Storing seeds in a seed bank
Breeding pandas in a zoo
Growing rare plants in a botanic garden
Setting up and managing a nature reserve in the species' natural habitat
questions.explanation: In situ means 'in place': species are protected in their natural habitat. Zoos, botanic gardens and seed banks are ex situ.

questions.text: Conserving species outside their natural habitat, for example in a zoo, is ___ conservation.
questions.explanation: Ex situ conservation protects species from threats in the wild and can support captive breeding and reintroduction.

questions.statement: Rewilding can involve reintroducing apex predators so that natural ecosystem processes are restored.
questions.explanation: Rewilding aims to restore self-sustaining ecosystems, e.g. reintroducing wolves to control herbivore numbers, with minimal ongoing human management.

questions.prompt: Match each conservation approach to an example.

pairs.right: Protecting a rainforest as a national park
Storing seeds of crop wild relatives in a seed bank

questions.explanation: Several approaches are needed because no single method works for every species or ecosystem.

questions.prompt: Why is protecting habitats (in situ) generally preferred to ex situ conservation where possible?
options: It requires no management
It conserves the species together with its ecosystem and interactions, and maintains natural behaviour and evolution
It guarantees the species will never go extinct
It allows unlimited hunting
questions.explanation: In situ conservation protects whole communities. Ex situ is useful when wild populations are critically threatened, but captive populations may lose natural behaviours and genetic diversity.

questions.prompt: What does the EDGE of Existence approach prioritise?
options: Species that are evolutionarily distinct, with few close relatives, and also globally endangered
Species that are most popular with the public
Species with the largest population sizes
Species that are economically valuable
questions.explanation: Losing an evolutionarily distinct species loses a unique branch of the tree of life, so these species are prioritised when they are also highly threatened.

questions.statement: Conservation resources are unlimited, so there is no need to select which species to prioritise.
questions.explanation: Funding and effort are limited, so approaches such as EDGE help decide which species to focus on.

questions.text: Restoring natural processes by reintroducing species and reducing human management is called ___.
questions.explanation: Rewilding focuses on restoring ecosystem processes rather than managing individual species.

questions.prompt: Why are several different approaches needed to conserve biodiversity?
options: Because each approach works for every species
Because only zoos are effective
Because threats and species' needs differ, and approaches complement each other
Because in situ conservation is illegal in many countries
questions.explanation: Some species need habitat protection, others captive breeding or seed banking, and degraded ecosystems may need rewilding; combining methods gives the best outcome.

questions.prompt: What is a key advantage of a seed bank for plant conservation?
options: Seeds stored there continue to evolve with their environment
It replaces the need to protect habitats
Seeds are released into the wild every year
Large numbers of seeds of many species can be stored for long periods in a small space at low temperature
questions.explanation: Dried, cold-stored seeds stay viable for decades, preserving genetic diversity as insurance against extinction in the wild. However, stored seeds do not evolve.
